abstracts.abstract: Traditional software quality models rely on linear decomposition approaches that fail to capture the emergent properties of large-scale software systems. This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework grounded in complex systems theory to fundamentally reimagine software quality assessment. We conceptualize software repositories as dynamic ecosystems where modules, developers, and their interactions form adaptive networks exhibiting self-organization and phase transitions. Our paradigm introduces the Software Ecosystem Complexity Index (SECI), which quantifies quality degradation through entropy measures derived from network topology evolution. The theoretical contributions include: (1) a formal mathematical model linking micro-level code changes to macro-level system behavior, (2) proof that software decay follows power-law distributions under specific connectivity conditions, and (3) identification of critical thresholds beyond which quality degradation becomes irreversible. Empirical validation across 2,847 open-source projects demonstrates that SECI predicts post-release defect density with 34% higher accuracy than conventional complexity metrics. This paradigm shift moves the software engineering discipline from reductionist quality models toward holistic ecosystem-based thinking, opening new research avenues in predictive maintenance and sustainable software evolution.

Technical debt management remains challenging due to the lack of rigorous quantification models that capture both immediate and long-term impacts on software quality. Existing approaches treat technical debt as a monolithic construct, missing critical nuances in how different debt types propagate through software architecture. This paper advances technical debt theory by introducing a multi-dimensional quantification framework that distinguishes architectural, code-level, and test debt with formal semantic relationships. Our model extends the classical economics-based debt metaphor by incorporating time-value decay functions and interest accumulation rates specific to each debt dimension. We formalize the debt propagation problem using graph-theoretic foundations, proving that architectural debt exhibits super-linear interest effects due to cross-cutting dependencies. The framework introduces the Debt Severity Index (DSI), enabling project managers to prioritize refactoring efforts based on predicted quality impact. Evaluation on 156 industrial systems spanning three application domains validates that our approach explains 28% more variance in maintenance effort than state-of-the-art technical debt tools. This contribution significantly advances software metrics theory by providing actionable quantification for a previously qualitative concept.

Software architecture design remains predominantly manual, relying on practitioner expertise rather than systematic optimization, leading to suboptimal structural decisions with long-term maintenance consequences. This paper introduces ArchGen, a paradigm-shifting generative system that synthesizes software architectures from high-level requirements specifications using constraint satisfaction and multi-objective optimization. Unlike existing model-driven development approaches that rely on templates or patterns, ArchGen treats architecture synthesis as a creative optimization problem, simultaneously considering quality attributes, domain constraints, and evolution projections. The system implements a novel hierarchical evolutionary algorithm that explores architectural alternatives at both component and connector levels, maintaining design rationale provenance throughout synthesis. Key architectural innovations include dynamic constraint relaxation for handling conflicting quality requirements and learned heuristics from 15,000 successful architectural patterns extracted from open-source repositories. We evaluated ArchGen through controlled experiments with 42 software architects, demonstrating that generated architectures achieve comparable quality scores while reducing design time by 67%. This work inaugurates a new paradigm where AI assists not merely in code generation but in fundamental architectural decision-making.

Automated code smell detection lacks integration between syntactic pattern matching and semantic understanding, resulting in high false positive rates that erode developer trust in software quality tools. Current static analysis approaches identify code anomalies through rule-based heuristics without contextualizing findings against architectural intent or historical evolution patterns. This paper presents SmellForge, an enhanced detection system that integrates abstract syntax tree analysis with graph neural networks trained on architectural quality dimensions. SmellForge addresses previous limitations through three significant improvements: (1) architectural context awareness that distinguishes acceptable patterns in legacy code from genuine quality violations, (2) temporal smell tracking that identifies whether detected issues are stable, regressing, or improving across versions, and (3) prioritization scoring that correlates smells with actual defect occurrences using learned embeddings. The system architecture employs a distributed processing pipeline enabling analysis of million-line codebases within practical timeframes. Empirical evaluation on 89 Java projects with verified defect reports demonstrates SmellForge achieves 23% higher precision and 18% better recall than SonarQube while maintaining comparable throughput. SmellForge provides actionable insights that bridge the gap between automated detection and meaningful refactoring decisions.
